Khách được trực tiếp tham gia vào bối cảnh lịch sử, thay vì chỉ đứng ngoài quan sát.
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: C. encourage visitors to become active participants . (Khuyến khích khách tham quan trở thành người tham gia chủ động .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: active participants move through it as though part of the scene Đáp án A “ Lần đầu hình thành tại các trung tâm ở Britain được nhắc đến ”: đoạn B nêu các trung tâm ở Britain như những ví dụ tiêu biểu (“fine instances”). Nhưng tác giả nói xu hướng bên kia Atlantic xuất hiện sớm hơn nhiều (“far sooner”). Đáp án B “ Phần lớn dựa vào hình ảnh do máy tính tạo ra ”: câu (6) nhắc máy tính (“computers”). Nhưng tác giả chỉ dự báo một hình thức sắp có, không khẳng định đây là phương thức chủ yếu. Đáp án D “ Chỉ phục vụ thị hiếu của một thiểu số nhỏ ”: nhóm phản đối (“Purists”) ở cuối đoạn B với nhóm yêu thích các hình thức mới. Nhưng phần đông không đồng tình với lời phản đối (“most people do not agree”), nên không thể kết luận chỉ một thiểu số hưởng ứng.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, theme parks, heritage sites and museums
options: are gradually becoming harder to tell apart.
have formed official partnerships with one another.
each strive to hold on to a separate identity.
now house broadly the same kinds of exhibit.
questions.correct: are gradually becoming harder to tell apart.

explanation.step1: According to the passage, theme parks, heritage sites and museums Câu hỏi hỏi: Bài đọc đưa ra nhận định nào đúng về ba loại hình: công viên chủ đề, khu di sản và bảo tàng?
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh để tìm chỗ nói về cả ba loại hình. Câu đầu đoạn C nhắc đến ranh giới (“line”) phân biệt bảo tàng và khu di sản với công viên chủ đề => bắt đầu đọc tại đây. Đoạn C — line
explanation.step3: Đoạn C: Alongside this runs a further shift: the once-firm line setting museums and heritage sites apart from theme parks is slowly fading . Ranh giới phân biệt đang mờ dần => ba loại hình ngày càng khó phân biệt .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: A. are gradually becoming harder to tell apart . ( Chúng đang dần trở nên khó phân biệt hơn .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: Ranh giới phân biệt is slowly fading ba loại hình are gradually becoming harder to tell apart Đáp án B “ Đã thiết lập quan hệ hợp tác chính thức với nhau ”: Nếu skim thấy việc vay mượn ý tưởng (“taking ideas and devices”) ở câu 2 đoạn C, dễ nghĩ đến hợp tác Nhưng ảnh hưởng lẫn nhau không có nghĩa là có quan hệ hợp tác chính thức. Đáp án C “ Mỗi loại hình đều cố giữ bản sắc riêng ”: Đoạn D có cụm nói về vai trò riêng biệt (“quite separate from the parks”), dễ gây nhầm Nhưng vai trò riêng không đồng nghĩa với nỗ lực giữ bản sắc riêng; bằng chứng đang nói ranh giới phân biệt mờ dần. Đáp án D “ Hiện trưng bày những loại hiện vật về cơ bản giống nhau ”: Sai vì khó phân biệt các loại hình không đồng nghĩa với việc chúng trưng bày cùng loại hiện vật. Bằng chứng không khẳng định nội dung trưng bày của cả ba giống nhau.

questions.prompt: The writer states that, in putting exhibits together, heritage specialists
options: should concentrate on a single aim.
have to translate a certain amount of text.
must weigh two opposing requirements against each other.
ought to be kept clear of commercial concerns.
questions.correct: must weigh two opposing requirements against each other.

explanation.step1: The writer states that , in putting exhibits together , heritage specialists Câu hỏi hỏi: Khi xây dựng phần trưng bày, các chuyên gia di sản phải đáp ứng yêu cầu gì?
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta tìm ý tương đương về công việc của chuyên gia di sản. Ở đoạn D, cụm diễn giải lịch sử (“the interpreting of history”) giúp nhận diện đúng nhóm người này => đây là vùng liên quan. Đoạn D — the interpreting of history
explanation.step3: Đoạn D: Anyone whose profession is the interpreting of history therefore occupies an awkward spot , obliged to hold a line between what the evidence will bear and what an audience finds attractive — all the more so as the heritage business faces mounting pressure to earn its keep . Gợi ý: Dấu hiệu thế khó càng tăng vì (“all the more so as”) chỉ mở rộng lý do; yêu cầu cân bằng đã rõ ở phần trước nên có thể bỏ qua phần xám. Chuyên gia phải cân bằng hai yêu cầu : trung thành với bằng chứng và tạo sức hấp dẫn đối với khán giả .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: C. must weigh two opposing requirements against each other . (Phải cân nhắc, dung hòa hai yêu cầu đối lập nhau.) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: must obliged weigh two opposing requirements against each other hold a line between + an awkward spot Đáp án A “ Nên tập trung vào một mục tiêu duy nhất ”: Sai vì câu (5) yêu cầu cân bằng cả hai phía, không phải chỉ theo đuổi một mục tiêu. Đáp án B “ Phải dịch một lượng văn bản nhất định ”: nhầm nếu hiểu từ diễn giải (“interpreting”) thành dịch ngôn ngữ. Nhưng ở đây tác giả nói về diễn giải lịch sử, không phải dịch văn bản. Đáp án D “ Nên được tách khỏi các mối quan tâm thương mại ”: Sai vì tác giả nêu yêu cầu cân bằng bằng chứng với sức hấp dẫn, chứ không đề nghị loại bỏ các cân nhắc thương mại.

questions.prompt: The writer's point in paragraph E is that certain museum displays
options: leave the people who view them disappointed.
reveal today's ways of thinking more than the reality of the past.
are built on the mistaken beliefs of the professionals.
give visitors freer rein to use their imagination.
questions.correct: reveal today's ways of thinking more than the reality of the past.

explanation.step1: The writer's point in paragraph E is that certain museum displays Câu hỏi hỏi: Tác giả nhận xét gì về một số cảnh trưng bày trong bảo tàng ở đoạn E? Lưu ý: đề không hỏi về mọi cách trưng bày.
explanation.step2: Đề đã chỉ rõ đoạn E. Ta bắt đầu ở ví dụ về hình phục dựng trong bảo tàng (“the reconstruction”), vì đây là một cảnh trưng bày cụ thể mà tác giả đưa ra để nhận xét. Đoạn E — the reconstruction
explanation.step3: Đoạn E: Take the reconstruction of an early human ancestor in a museum on the island of Sabalu , its figure given distinctly local features because that is what the public expects ; or the display at the National Museum of Prehistory in Aldermont, where a prehistoric man is posed making a domineering gesture towards his mate . What such scenes reveal is less about those who came before us than about how the present-day world sees things . Câu (2): nêu ví dụ hình phục dựng mang nét địa phương theo kỳ vọng của công chúng. Câu (3): từ ví dụ đó, khái quát rằng các cảnh trưng bày phản ánh cách nhìn hiện tại nhiều hơn thực tế quá khứ .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: B. reveal today's ways of thinking more than the reality of the past . (Phản ánh cách nghĩ ngày nay nhiều hơn thực tế quá khứ .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: today's ways of thinking how the present day world sees things more than the reality of the past less about those who came before us cùng hướng so sánh, nhưng đảo thứ tự hai phía. Đáp án A “ Khiến người xem thất vọng ”: Sai vì tác giả đang so sánh điều các cảnh trưng bày phản ánh, không nhận xét về cảm giác thất vọng của người xem. Đáp án C “ Được xây dựng trên những niềm tin sai lầm của các chuyên gia ”: Nếu scan câu 4 đoạn E thấy lỗi lầm và định kiến (“errors and prejudices”), bạn dễ chọn nhầm Nhưng đó là những yếu tố trong cách diễn giải do khách tham quan tự tạo ra, không phải niềm tin của chuyên gia. Đáp án D “ Cho khách tham quan tự do tưởng tượng hơn ”: Câu 4 đoạn E có ý khách tham quan sẽ tự đưa ra cách diễn giải (“visitors would supply their own”) Nhưng điều này chỉ xảy ra trong giả định không cung cấp diễn giải, không phải tác dụng của các cảnh trưng bày đang được hỏi.

questions.prompt: The passage closes by explaining that our picture of the past is distorted because
options: we make too little use of our own imagination.
we choose to look past whatever troubles us.
exhibitions dwell too heavily on the surrounding region.
only the sturdiest objects have survived the years.
questions.correct: only the sturdiest objects have survived the years.

explanation.step1: The passage closes by explaining that our picture of the past is distorted because Câu hỏi hỏi: Phần kết bài nêu nguyên nhân nào khiến hình dung của chúng ta về quá khứ bị sai lệch?
explanation.step2: Chỉ dẫn phần kết bài (“The passage closes”) đưa ta đến đoạn F. Bắt đầu đọc tại chỗ tác giả nêu một sự sai lệch thứ hai (“a second distortion”) và giải thích nguyên nhân của nó. Đoạn F — The passage closes
explanation.step3: Đoạn F: If human bias cannot be escaped , a second distortion in how history reaches us stems from the perishable character of the materials that come down to us . Vật liệu kém bền dễ mất đi => những gì còn lại thiên về các đồ vật bền chắc , không đại diện đầy đủ cho quá khứ.
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: D. only the sturdiest objects have survived the years . ( Chỉ những đồ vật bền chắc nhất mới tồn tại qua năm tháng .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: stems from because Đáp án A “ Chúng ta vận dụng trí tưởng tượng quá ít ”: Sai vì nguyên nhân được nêu là tính dễ hư hỏng của vật liệu, không phải việc thiếu trí tưởng tượng. Đáp án B “ Chúng ta chủ động bỏ qua những điều khiến mình khó chịu ”: Đoạn F nhắc cảm giác hoài niệm (“a wave of nostalgia”), dễ khiến ta nghĩ người xem né tránh mặt khó chịu của quá khứ Nhưng đó là phản ứng trước trưng bày, không phải hành động cố tình bỏ qua sự thật. Đáp án C “ Các cuộc trưng bày quá tập trung vào khu vực xung quanh ”: Đoạn E có đặc điểm địa phương (“distinctly local features”), dễ kéo ta về option này Nhưng phần kết bài giải thích sự sai lệch do độ bền của vật liệu, không phải phạm vi địa lý của trưng bày.

questions.prompt: The way zoos now keep their animals is regarded as one of the most important changes of the twentieth century in the way the natural world is shown.

explanation.step1: The way zoos now keep their animals is regarded as one of the most important changes of the twentieth century in the way the natural world is shown . Ý câu hỏi: Cách sở thú hiện giữ động vật được xem là một trong những thay đổi quan trọng nhất của thế kỷ XX trong việc trưng bày thế giới tự nhiên.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh để tìm phần nói về cách giữ động vật tại sở thú. Đoạn C có ý sở thú cũng thay đổi tương tự (“Zoos tell a similar story”) => đây là điểm bắt đầu đọc kĩ. Đoạn C — Zoos tell a similar story
explanation.step3: Đoạn C: Zoos tell a similar story : rather than being shut in cages , their animals are given generous room , whether outdoors or inside vast glasshouses — the tropical and arid habitats recreated at Meervenn Zoo in Belgium are a case in point . Among the twentieth century's leading changes in how the natural world is displayed , this shift is often ranked among the most important . Câu (4): nêu thay đổi ở sở thú: từ nhốt động vật trong lồng sang dành không gian rộng . Câu (5): đánh giá thay đổi ấy thuộc nhóm quan trọng nhất của thế kỷ XX trong cách trưng bày thế giới tự nhiên.
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: cách giữ động vật hiện nay tại sở thú được xem là một trong những thay đổi quan trọng nhất (“ one of the most important changes ”) của thế kỷ XX trong việc trưng bày thế giới tự nhiên. Bài đọc nói: thay đổi này (“ this shift ”) — tức cách giữ động vật ở sở thú trong câu (4) — thường được xếp vào nhóm quan trọng nhất (“often ranked among the most important ”), đúng thời gian và lĩnh vực mà câu hỏi nêu. Hai ý cùng nghĩa ; bài đọc xác nhận nhận định . Đáp án đúng: TRUE Đối chiếu paraphrasing: is regarded as is often ranked one of the most important changes among the most important the way the natural world is shown how the natural world is displayed FALSE Sai vì câu (5) trực tiếp xếp thay đổi này vào nhóm quan trọng nhất, không đưa ra đánh giá ngược lại. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài nói thay đổi này không thuộc nhóm quan trọng nhất của thế kỷ XX trong lĩnh vực đó. NOT GIVEN nhầm nếu không biết thay đổi này (“this shift”) chỉ điều gì Nhưng cụm này nhắc lại cách giữ động vật ở câu (4), nên bài đã có đánh giá về sở thú. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài chỉ mô tả thay đổi mà không đánh giá tầm quan trọng của nó.

questions.prompt: Museums draw larger numbers of visitors than theme parks do.

explanation.step1: Museums draw larger numbers of visitors than theme parks do . Ý câu hỏi: Bảo tàng thu hút nhiều khách hơn công viên giải trí.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh để tìm thông tin về mối quan hệ giữa bảo tàng và công viên giải trí. Câu 2 đoạn D đề cập vai trò và áp lực thị trường của hai loại hình này => đây là vùng liên quan. Đoạn D
explanation.step3: Đoạn D: Market pressure lies behind the move ; and while museums and heritage sites fill a role of their own , quite separate from the parks , they too must survive in a crowded marketplace where people decide freely how, and where, to pass their leisure hours .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Bảo tàng thu hút nhiều khách hơn công viên giải trí. Bài đọc nói: Bảo tàng có vai trò riêng, nhưng cũng phải tồn tại trong thị trường cạnh tranh. Bài không so sánh lượng khách giữa hai bên. Có nhắc đến cả hai loại hình, nhưng thiếu thông tin để xác định bên nào đông khách hơn . Đáp án đúng: NOT GIVEN Đối chiếu paraphrasing: larger numbers of visitors than theme parks do không có trong bài. Đáp án TRUE Nếu chỉ thấy ý thu hút đám đông (“draw a crowd”) ở câu 3 đoạn D, dễ chọn TRUE Nhưng thu hút được khách không chứng minh nhiều khách hơn công viên giải trí. Chỉ chọn TRUE nếu bài xác nhận bảo tàng thu hút nhiều khách hơn công viên giải trí. FALSE Đoạn B nhắc sự phổ biến (“popularity”) của công viên giải trí, dễ khiến ta suy ra nơi này đông khách hơn Nhưng phổ biến không chứng minh lượng khách lớn hơn hoặc bằng bảo tàng. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài xác nhận bảo tàng có ít khách hơn hoặc lượng khách bằng công viên giải trí.

questions.prompt: The writer thinks experts produce a less distorted account than visitors would arrive at on their own.

explanation.step1: The writer thinks experts produce a less distorted account than visitors would arrive at on their own . Ý câu hỏi: Cách diễn giải của chuyên gia ít sai lệch hơn cách khách tham quan tự hình thành . Không cần chứng minh chuyên gia hoàn toàn không có sai lệch.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh để tìm ý so sánh cách diễn giải của chuyên gia với cách khách tham quan tự hình thành. Ở đoạn E, ý khách tự đưa ra cách diễn giải (“visitors would supply their own”) cho biết đây là vùng liên quan. Đoạn E — visitors would supply their own
explanation.step3: Đoạn E: Yet the interpreters can claim one point in their favour: withhold the interpretation , and visitors would supply their own , drawing on personal notions, errors and prejudices — and however lively that home-made version, it would carry far more distortion than the experts' work .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Bản diễn giải của chuyên gia ít sai lệch hơn bản khách tự hình thành (“less distorted”). Bài đọc nói: Bản khách tự hình thành sai lệch nhiều hơn bản của chuyên gia (“ more distortion than the experts' work ”). => Cùng một quan hệ so sánh , chỉ đổi phía được nói đến. Hai ý trùng khớp . Đáp án đúng: True Đối chiếu paraphrasing: arrive at on their own supply their own experts produce a less distorted account more distortion than the experts' work — phía bài đọc đang nói về bản của khách. FALSE Đầu đoạn E có ý bẻ cong sự thật lịch sử (“bending of historical truth”), dễ khiến ta nghĩ chuyên gia diễn giải sai nên chọn FALSE Nhưng có sai lệch không đồng nghĩa với sai lệch hơn khách. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài nói khách tự diễn giải ít sai lệch hơn chuyên gia. NOT GIVEN Nếu chỉ tìm đúng cụm ít sai lệch hơn (“less distorted”), ta dễ bỏ sót phép so sánh theo chiều ngược lại trong bài Nhưng câu (4) đã nói rõ bản của khách sai lệch nhiều hơn bản chuyên gia, nên thông tin không bị thiếu. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài nói cả hai bên đều có thiên kiến nhưng không cho biết bên nào sai lệch hơn.

questions.prompt: The grand rooms from earlier centuries that museums display represent the homes of poorer households.

explanation.step1: The grand rooms from earlier centuries that museums display represent the homes of poorer households . Ý câu hỏi: Những căn phòng cổ được trưng bày phản ánh nhà ở của các hộ nghèo hơn .
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh để tìm thông tin về những căn phòng cổ trong bảo tàng. Ở đoạn F, cụm những căn phòng trang nhã (“The elegant rooms”) giúp xác định vùng cần đọc kĩ. Đoạn F — The elegant rooms
explanation.step3: Đoạn F: The elegant rooms of that era preserved in museums , however, conjure up only how the wealthy lived .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Những căn phòng này đại diện cho nhà ở của các hộ nghèo hơn (“poorer households”). Bài đọc nói: Những căn phòng này chỉ gợi lại cuộc sống của người giàu (“ only how the wealthy lived ”). => Hai thông tin mâu thuẫn trực tiếp về nhóm người mà những căn phòng phản ánh. Đáp án đúng: FALSE Đối chiếu paraphrasing: the homes of poorer households only how the wealthy lived Đáp án TRUE Nếu skim/scan thấy những căn phòng trang nhã (“elegant rooms”) và bảo tàng, sẽ dễ chọn TRUE Nhưng đúng đối tượng chưa đủ: bài nói về người giàu, không phải các hộ nghèo hơn. Chỉ chọn TRUE nếu bài nói những căn phòng ấy phản ánh nhà ở của các hộ nghèo hơn. NOT GIVEN Nếu chỉ tìm nguyên văn cụm các hộ nghèo hơn (“poorer households”), sẽ dễ chọn NOT GIVEN Nhưng bài đã xác định rõ những căn phòng chỉ phản ánh cuộc sống của người giàu, đủ để bác bỏ nhận định. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài không cho biết những căn phòng phản ánh cuộc sống của nhóm người nào.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man asking about a part-time job at a restaurant. First you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:47] WOMAN: Good evening King's restaurant. How can I help?
[00:51] MAN: Good evening. I'm calling about the vacancy I've heard you have.
[00:55] WOMAN: Yes, that's right.
[00:57] MAN: I'd like to ask for a few more details if that's all right.
[01:02] WOMAN: Of course. Could I take your name first?
[01:06] MAN: Peter Chin.
[01:07] WOMAN: Thanks Peter. Ask whatever you need to know and if the position still suits you we can arrange an interview.
[01:15] MAN: Great. I didn't see the advertisement myself. A friend told me about it.
[01:21] WOMAN: That's absolutely fine. What would you like to know?
[01:25] MAN: First, what does the work involve? Is it washing dishes?
[01:30] WOMAN: No, the main duty is answering the phone rather than serving at the tables.
[01:37] MAN: That sounds suitable. How many evenings would I work each week?
[01:41] WOMAN: The restaurant is busiest at weekends.
[01:44] MAN: So would that mean two evenings?
[01:47] WOMAN: Actually, it would be three making 12 hours altogether each week.
[01:51] MAN: Fine. That shouldn't affect my studies.
[01:54] WOMAN: Are you studying at the university?
[01:56] MAN: Yes, I'm a first-year physics student as I'm not from the EU. Would I need a work permit?
[02:03] WOMAN: You would. Your tutor just needs to sign it.
[02:07] MAN: That should be easy to arrange. Which restaurant is the vacancy at?
[02:12] WOMAN: We have two branches, but this job is at the Hills Dunne Road one.
[02:16] MAN: I'm not familiar with that name. Could you spell it?
[02:21] WOMAN: Certainly. H. I. Double L.
[02:25] WOMAN: S. D. U. Double N.
[02:29] WOMAN: E. Then road.
[02:32] MAN: Thank you. Is there a bus stop nearby?
[02:35] WOMAN: Yes, the closest stop is beside the library.
[02:39] MAN: I know where that is. And what is the hourly rate?
[02:44] WOMAN: We pay £4.45 an hour.
[02:46] MAN: That's good. My previous job only paid £3.95. We think it's competitive, and there are some useful additional benefits too. Such as?
[02:58] WOMAN: You receive a free dinner during your shift.
[03:02] MAN: Better than the food at my hostel, then?
[03:04] WOMAN: I hope so. We also pay a higher rate if you work on national holidays.
[03:10] MAN: That's a worthwhile benefit.
[03:11] WOMAN: And because public transport becomes difficult late at night, we'll take you home if your shift finishes after 11 o'clock.
[03:20] MAN: That's reassuring.
[03:23] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
[04:08] WOMAN: If you're still interested, we'd be happy to invite you for an interview.
[04:12] MAN: I certainly am. Before we arrange it, what qualities do you need?
[04:18] WOMAN: For this role, a clear voice is essential, and yours is certainly clear.
[04:23] MAN: Thank you.
[04:24] WOMAN: You also need to be able to think quickly when you're dealing with callers.
[04:28] MAN: I believe I can do that.
[04:31] WOMAN: When could you come in? We're fairly quiet this evening.
[04:35] MAN: I can't manage tonight or tomorrow, I'm afraid. Thursday would work. That's the 22nd of October.
[04:43] WOMAN: Any time after 5?
[04:45] MAN: Yes. Would 6 o'clock be convenient?
[04:49] WOMAN: Perfect. Please bring the names of two referees.
[04:53] MAN: No problem. Who should I ask for when I arrive?
[04:57] WOMAN: Ask for me. My name is Samira Manuja.
[05:01] MAN: Would you spell the surname, please?
[05:04] WOMAN: M-A-N-U-J-A.
[05:06] MAN: Got it. Thank you very much.
[05:08] WOMAN: You're welcome. I look forward to meeting you.
[05:14] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Course Feedback
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Course Feedback"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a teacher talking with two students about an English for academic purposes course. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

[00:51] TEACHER: Before we begin, Spiros and Hiroko, thank you for coming to discuss your recent academic experiences and congratulations to both of you on such good results in your first semester examinations. I'd like your views on the English for academic purposes course you completed here last year before entering university. Spiros, let's start with you. Which parts of that programme have been most useful since you began your degree?

[01:26] SPIROS: Having to give a seminar presentation helped a great deal. A couple of weeks ago, I presented in our marketing course and I felt reasonably confident because I had done it before and knew what was involved. I was still nervous, of course, but I had prepared thoroughly and practiced the timing. Compared with several people in my group, I think I performed well because my delivery came across as polished and well organised.
[01:55] SPIROS: How was it for you, Hiroko?

[01:57] HIROKO: That's interesting. I was astonished by the way other students in my group presented. They simply read their notes aloud. They paid very little attention to delivery and barely looked up at the people listening, even though our previous course had placed considerable emphasis on those skills.
[02:20] TEACHER: What did you do in your own presentation, Hiroko?
[02:23] HIROKO: Honestly, I read from my notes as well. It felt easier while I was doing it, but afterwards I had no real feeling of achievement. I came away disappointed with how it had gone.

[02:37] SPIROS: That's unfortunate. Although I was pleased with my presentation, I'm not at all pleased with how I've performed in tutorials. I haven't contributed to the discussions at any point this semester.
[02:49] HIROKO: Really? Is that because the other students dominate the conversation?

[02:54] SPIROS: That's part of it, but the main issue is that I haven't had the confidence to join in. Their way of speaking is very different from what we practiced. They use a lot of informal expressions, aren't always particularly polite, and the discussion can seem disorganised. They've known each other for some time.
[03:14] SPIROS: Because they understand each other's habits, they know when to bring someone else into the conversation.
[03:23] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

[04:08] HIROKO: I've had the same experience. For most of the semester I contributed nothing in tutorials. Recently though, I've made myself speak up and simply enter the discussion. That has made me feel much more positive because I'm taking a more active part.
[04:26] HIROKO: I've also noticed that when the others consider one of my ideas interesting or original, they ask for my opinion the next time. After that, joining the discussion becomes much easier.
[04:40] SPIROS: That's encouraging. I hope I can achieve that next semester. I'll need to find some worthwhile points to raise. What helped you develop your ideas?

[04:51] HIROKO: Reading was important. This semester I've had to read extensively just to understand the lectures. At first, the lecturer's explanations made little sense to me, so I turned to textbooks and published research papers. I spent hours reading each evening, following the reference lists we were given and producing pages of notes.
[05:15] HIROKO: I reviewed those notes again over breakfast. This routine has helped me follow the lectures and has supplied ideas for tutorials.
[05:25] SPIROS: I already do so much reading that I can't imagine adding anything else. My reading is still quite slow, although handling unfamiliar vocabulary is easier than it used to be.
[05:39] TEACHER: What could we add to the course to address that reading difficulty?

[05:43] SPIROS: I'm not sure the course could do more because the problem is mine. We were assigned long articles which we disliked at the time, but I now realise they prepared us well for university reading. We also completed regular speed reading activities and kept records of our pace, so the teachers did encourage us to improve.

[06:06] HIROKO: That's true, but the choice of material could have been different. In English classes, I sometimes became frustrated with articles about the environment, health or education. I'm studying to become an engineer, yet we read nothing connected with it. I felt I was spending time on vocabulary I didn't need.
[06:29] TEACHER: Weren't the strategies for dealing with that vocabulary still valuable?
[06:33] HIROKO: Yes, but I would have felt more confident if the text had related to what I'm studying. What do you think, Spiros?

[06:41] SPIROS: I agree. Texts related to our degrees would have increased my confidence and motivation too. It was helpful though that our research assignments could be based on topics we chose ourselves.
[06:56] TEACHER: Alright, let's turn now to writing.
[07:00] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: Mass Stranding Of Whales And Dolphins
content: 📌 Mass stranding of whales and dolphins
Mass strandings
Groups of marine mammals come ashore and die.They are frequent where the [ _____ ] may alter rapidly.
Possible explanations
Parasites
Parasites can damage an animal's [ _____ ], which is essential for navigation.
Toxins
Whales commonly consume poisons originating in [ _____ ].In 1988, saxitoxin killed whales at Cape Cod.
Accidental strandings
Animals may chase prey onto shore, as observed by Thurston in 1995.This is doubtful because most animals were not [ _____ ] when they stranded.
Human activity
[ _____ ] produced by military tests have been associated with recent cases.The Bahamas event in 2000 was unusual because the whales:were all [ _____ ] were not together in a [ _____ ].
Group behaviour
Strandings occur more often among the most [ _____ ] whale species.In the 1994 dolphin case, only the [ _____ ] was sick.
Further reading
Connor's Marine Mammals Ashore provides information about stranding [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing possible causes of mass strandings of whales and dolphins. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Good afternoon.

[00:55] AUDIO: Since some of you will soon begin fieldwork, today's topic is especially relevant. I want to consider why groups of whales and dolphins sometimes leave the sea, move onto a beach and, in most cases, die. These events are known as mass strandings. Sadly, strandings occur frequently in several of the places you will visit.

[01:19] AUDIO: In some such locations, the tide can change very quickly, leaving the animals confused. However, researchers have proposed a number of other explanations. One theory connects strandings with parasites. Large infestations are often discovered in stranded animals.

[01:41] AUDIO: For example, worms are commonly found in the ears of dead whales. Marine mammals depend heavily on their hearing to navigate, so parasites affecting it can cause serious harm. A second explanation concerns toxins, or poisons, which have contributed to many marine animal deaths. Such toxins may originate in plants or animals and are then consumed by whales during normal feeding.

[02:13] AUDIO: Whether they lead directly or indirectly to stranding seems to depend on the particular poison. In 1988, 14 humpback whales that stranded along Cape Cod were examined. They had eaten tuna containing saxetoxin, a substance that can also be fatal to people. Some researchers have suggested that animals may strand by accident while pursuing prey close to shore.

[02:43] AUDIO: In 1995, David Thurston observed pilot whales beaching after they had followed squid. Yet, this explanation is unlikely to account for most mass strandings. Analysis of stomach contents shows that the majority of the animals were not feeding at the time. More recent theories connect strandings with human activity.

[03:12] AUDIO: One increasing concern is that powerful noise in the ocean can cause such events. Sounds generated during military tests have been linked in particular with several recent strandings. A case in the Bahamas in 2000 occurred at almost exactly the same time as trials of a new submarine detection system. Several unusual features led scientists to search for a new cause.

[03:40] AUDIO: First, every stranded whale was healthy. Second, the animals were distributed along 38 kilometres of coastline rather than being together in a group, as normally happens in a mass stranding. The final theory involves social behaviour. It proposes that marine mammals cannot tell whether a leader is healthy or sick and will continue following an ill leader even when doing so is fatal.

[04:12] AUDIO: This explanation is particularly interesting because the whale species considered most social, namely toothed whales, are also those that strand most often. Evidence from a dolphin stranding in 1994 supports the theory. Examinations showed that only the leader had been ill while all the other dolphins were healthy. Because no single explanation accounts for every case, our immediate options are limited to helping animals whenever possible.

[04:50] AUDIO: Stranding networks now operate around the world, rescuing survivors and collecting samples from animals that cannot be saved. For anyone wanting to learn more about these networks, or perhaps establish one, John Connor's book Marine Mammals Assure is an excellent place to begin. That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

content: 📌 Accommodation form

Type of accommodation: hall of residence
Name: Anu [ _____ ]
Date of birth: [ _____ ]
Country of origin: India
Course of study: [ _____ ]
Number of years planned in hall: [ _____ ]
Preferred catering arrangement: half board
Special dietary requirement: no red [ _____ ]
Preferred room: a single [ _____ ]
Interests: the [ _____ ] and badminton
Priorities when choosing a hall
To live with students who are [ _____ ]To be outside the [ _____ ]To have a [ _____ ] social area
Contact telephone number: 667549
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a student discussing accommodation with a university officer. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:50] MAN: Good morning. How can I help?
[00:53] WOMAN: I've recently been accepted onto a university course, and I'd like to arrange a room in a hall of residence.
[00:59] MAN: Certainly. Please take a seat. I'll complete a form with you so we can record your circumstances and preferences.
[01:09] WOMAN: Thank you.
[01:10] MAN: Let's begin with your name.
[01:12] WOMAN: It's Anubhat.
[01:14] MAN: Could you spell that, please?
[01:17] WOMAN: A, N, U, then B, H, A, double T.
[01:23] MAN: Thank you. What's your date of birth?
[01:26] WOMAN: The 31st of March, 1972.
[01:30] MAN: And which country are you from?
[01:33] WOMAN: India.
[01:34] MAN: What subject will you be studying?
[01:38] WOMAN: Nursing.
[01:39] MAN: How many years do you expect to live in a hall?
[01:43] WOMAN: The course lasts three years, but I'd only like hall accommodation for two. In my final year, I'd prefer to consider living elsewhere.
[01:53] MAN: Fine. What catering arrangement would you like? You could prepare all your own food or choose full board, where every meal is included.
[02:05] WOMAN: Is there an option between those two?
[02:08] MAN: Yes. Half board provides the evening meal only.
[02:13] WOMAN: That would suit me best.
[02:15] MAN: Many students choose it. Do you have any dietary requirements we need to record?
[02:22] WOMAN: Yes. I don't eat red meat.

[02:26] MAN: No red meat. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Now, regarding the room, there are several choices.

[03:22] MAN: We offer either single or shared study bedrooms, which are our standard rooms. Alternatively, a single bedsit provides extra space and better facilities, although it costs about 20 pounds more each week.
[03:40] WOMAN: My grant is fairly generous, so I'd choose the bedsit.
[03:44] MAN: Good. I'll note that, and we'll check availability. May I ask about your interests? This information can help us place you in a suitable hall.
[03:57] WOMAN: I love the theatre, and I also enjoy sport, especially badminton.
[04:03] MAN: That's useful. The final part of the form concerns your priorities when choosing a hall. We'll try to take them into account.
[04:13] WOMAN: Most importantly, I'd like to live with other mature students if possible.
[04:17] MAN: We do have halls that tend to accommodate older students.
[04:23] WOMAN: I'd also prefer somewhere outside the town.
[04:26] MAN: That should help, because halls outside town usually have more vacancies.
[04:32] WOMAN: That's fortunate.
[04:34] MAN: Anything else?
[04:36] WOMAN: I'd like a shared area for socializing, perhaps a television room or something similar.
[04:42] MAN: That's certainly a good way to meet people.
[04:45] WOMAN: Those are all my preferences.
[04:48] MAN: We just need a contact telephone number now.
[04:51] WOMAN: It's double six seven five four nine.
[04:54] MAN: Excellent. We'll contact you as soon as we can.
[05:03] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a speaker welcoming new members to a wildlife club. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 13. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 13. Hello, and welcome to our wildlife club.

[00:54] AUDIO: I'm delighted that you share our interest in the local countryside and its plants and animals. Although this area is quite close to London, it supports a surprising variety of wildlife. I'll begin with several nearby parks and open spaces. Halland Common is a particularly pleasant place.

[01:17] AUDIO: It has belonged to the public for centuries and the river Ouse begins there before flowing 80 km to the sea. An information board describes the plants and animals visitors may encounter and the common is accessible at any hour of the day. Holt Island is best known for its wide variety of trees. Willows were once cultivated commercially there for basket making and people have recently revived that traditional craft.

[01:47] AUDIO: The island admits visitors only from Friday through Sunday. Because it is small, opening every day would disturb much of its wildlife. A short walk over the bridge brings you to Longfield Country Park. The park contains a modern reconstruction of a farm dating from more than 2000 years ago.

[02:10] AUDIO: It often runs children's activities such as bread making and face painting. Remember that Longfield is open only during daylight. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 14 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 14 to 20.

[03:08] AUDIO: Longfield Park offers activities throughout the year. Here is a sample from the coming week. On Monday, visitors can explore how herbs have been used over many centuries. The session begins with a tour of the herb garden, followed by practical work using herbs to dye fabric.

[03:30] AUDIO: There will also be an illustrated presentation about their role in food and medicine. On Wednesday evening, local specialists will help visitors identify the insects and birds that become active after dark. Numbers are deliberately kept low, so anyone wishing to attend must telephone the park ranger several days beforehand. A small fee is payable on arrival.

[03:57] AUDIO: On Saturday, you can help maintain the park by joining a working group. Tasks range from planting hedges to collecting litter, and participants may move between activities. The rangers will work all day, but visitors are welcome to help for a shorter period. Please wear clothes that can safely become dirty or torn.

[04:21] AUDIO: Finally, I'd like to introduce the new wildlife area at Hinchingbrook Park, which opens to the public next month. The plan doesn't convey its full size, but it shows both entrances and the principal paths. A lake lies in the northwest, and the bird hide is immediately west of it, at the end of a path. It should provide a peaceful place to observe birds on the water.

[04:48] AUDIO: The dog walking area is in the southern part of the park, close to the refreshment point and leading off the path. Visitors who simply want to rest can use the flower garden, the circular space enclosed by paths. The wooded area is in the western section, positioned between two paths. That's all from me, so let's continue with...
[05:16] AUDIO: That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

Sau khi có mốc lake , nghe tiếp cụm “immediately west of it” : west of it = nằm về phía tây / bên trái của lake immediately = ngay sát , không phải ở xa Audio còn nói thêm “at the end of a path” → vị trí đúng phải là điểm cuối của một lối đi , không phải nằm giữa đường. Trên bản đồ, chỉ có A nằm bên trái hồ và ở cuối một nhánh đườ

passages.title: Self-Access Centre
content: Equipment
Replace the computers to provide additional space.
Resources
Make the level of the [ _____ ] materials clearer.Modernise the [ _____ ] collection.Purchase some [ _____ ] and separate them into pages.
Use of the room
Consult the teachers and prepare a [ _____ ] for supervision.Fit an [ _____ ].Limit personal use of [ _____ ] on the computers.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear the Director of Studies discussing a self-access centre with a student representative. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.

[00:54] PAM: Hello John, I've invited you here to discuss what should happen to our self-access centre. We need to decide the future of this important facility for our English language students. What are the students' views?

[01:09] JUN: They definitely want to retain it. Most students enjoy the centre because it provides a change from ordinary classroom work. And they consider it an important element of their course. However, they would like improved equipment, especially computers.
[01:26] JUN: At present, there aren't enough machines for everyone, so students must share.

[01:33] PAM: The teachers also recognise its value. However, many students use the computers for personal email. We don't want to prevent access, but these machines should primarily support learning. Some teachers believe the centre would be more effective if it were moved into the main university library.
[01:55] PAM: How would students respond to that suggestion?

[01:59] JUN: The library certainly has sufficient space, but visiting it wouldn't feel like a class activity. Our greatest concern is that students might have difficulty getting advice from a teacher. There would probably be plenty of resources, but learners need guidance when selecting suitable activities.
[02:19] PAM: A teacher would still be present to direct students rather than leaving them entirely alone.

[02:26] JUN: Even so, students would prefer the present arrangement. They like attending the centre with their teacher and completing activities together. If we improve the equipment and resources, the existing centre would work well. Would the cost be a problem?

[02:44] PAM: Expense isn't my main concern, and there is enough room. The difficulty is arranging for a teacher to supervise the centre outside lesson times. If we invest heavily in resources and equipment, someone must ensure they are properly looked after.
[03:06] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.

[03:53] PAM: Let's make a list of the changes the centre needs. We could begin by replacing the computers with newer models. They occupy less room, which would create more working space for books and other materials.
[04:08] JUN: That would help. The room can feel crowded.
[04:12] PAM: What improvements do students want in the other resources?
[04:16] JUN: They often struggle to identify material appropriate to their ability, especially the reading resources. The different levels should be labelled more clearly.
[04:28] PAM: That can be organised quickly. We should probably review all the study materials because some are becoming outdated.
[04:36] JUN: I agree. The CD collection particularly needs updating. We should buy the recordings that accompany our newest course books and obtain several copies.

[04:48] PAM: I was also considering a type of resource we don't currently provide – workbooks. We could separate them into individual pages and laminate those pages. Students would use the principal course book in class, then complete additional practice in the centre.
[05:08] JUN: That sounds useful.

[05:11] PAM: Finally, we should consider how the room is managed. I'll consult the teachers and arrange a timetable for supervision after classes. Security is also important if we buy expensive new equipment.
[05:25] JUN: Could we install an alarm?
[05:27] PAM: Good suggestion. I'd also like our technicians to find a way of restricting access to personal email. I don't want the facilities being misused.
[05:38] JUN: Perhaps students could use email only before and after lessons.
[05:42] PAM: That would be acceptable. Good, that's enough for now. We can continue once we've managed to.
[05:52] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer describing several types of organizational culture. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Good morning.

[00:52] AUDIO: Whether you plan to study business at university or choose another discipline, many of you will eventually work for some form of company. When you enter an organization, you'll soon notice that it has particular social characteristics. We call these its culture, the unwritten assumptions, beliefs, and values that shape how it operates. One influential writer divided organizational cultures into four main types.

[01:23] AUDIO: The first is power culture, usually associated with small organizations. To operate successfully, it requires a central source of power. Because control rests with only one or two individuals, the organization has relatively few formal rules or procedures. Communication generally occurs through conversations rather than written memoranda or official meetings.

[01:51] AUDIO: An advantage of this culture is speed. The business can respond rapidly both to threats and to new opportunities. Its weakness is that it may not always act effectively. The organization depends heavily on the few people at the top, and if they make poor decisions, others have little influence over them.

[02:14] AUDIO: Employees suited to this culture are comfortable taking risks and place little importance on job security. The second type is role culture. That's role, R-O-L-E, rather than role. It normally appears in large companies containing many different levels.

[02:36] AUDIO: Such organizations have specialist departments responsible for areas such as finance, sales, and maintenance. A small senior management group coordinates those departments, while rules and procedures define individual jobs. These include formal job descriptions and disciplinary regulations. This culture offers several benefits.

[03:00] AUDIO: In a large organization, fixed costs are low in relation to total output, producing economies of scale. It also succeeds in markets where technical ability is particularly important. However, role culture is often slow to recognize when change is necessary and slower still to respond. It suits employees who value security and prefer not to accept responsibility.

[03:28] AUDIO: The third category is task culture, found in organizations structured around projects. It commonly develops where markets are highly competitive or products have short lives. Senior managers assign projects, staff, and other resources. Once those have been allocated, they exercise little daily control because intervening would be seen as violating the system.

[03:55] AUDIO: A major advantage of task culture is that it is flexible. However, it cannot easily achieve economies of scale or develop great depth of expertise. People who enjoy working in teams tend to prefer this culture. Finally, the fourth category is known as person culture.
[04:19] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

[02:53] MAN: The apartments don't provide it. Although you should find it elsewhere in Arilas, satellite television is available too.
[03:02] WOMAN: And the price?
[03:03] MAN: Four hundred ninety pounds when two people share.
[03:07] WOMAN: So that is two hundred forty five pounds per person?
[03:10] MAN: No. I'm afraid each guest pays four hundred ninety pounds and an apartment must be occupied by at least two people.
[03:20] WOMAN: That is beyond our budget. The last place also sounds expensive. The Grand.
[03:27] MAN: Surprisingly, it is quite affordable. It is an older house with Greek paintings in every room and a balcony outside.
[03:36] WOMAN: What can you see from it?
[03:37] MAN: The building looks out over forests. They partly hide a supermarket just down the road, which is useful for shopping. And there is a disco nearby.
[03:50] WOMAN: What would it cost?
[03:51] MAN: Three hundred nineteen pounds for the period you want. In November, it becomes forty percent cheaper.
[03:59] WOMAN: November would be too late for us.
[04:01] MAN: I could post you a brochure with all the details, Ms. Nash.
[04:06] WOMAN: There's no need, though. I'll be in Upminster soon so I can collect one. For now, I only wanted a general idea.
[04:14] MAN: That's fine. We have plenty of brochures here.
[04:21] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions six to ten. Now listen and answer questions six to ten.
[05:06] WOMAN: While I have you, may I ask about insurance? I received another policy by post, but I want to compare it with yours.
[05:16] MAN: Certainly. What would you like to check?
[05:19] WOMAN: The policy lists each benefit and the largest amount that can be claimed. Does yours work the same way?
[05:27] MAN: Yes, that is the usual arrangement.
[05:30] WOMAN: For cancellation, the policy I have pays up to eight thousand pounds.
[05:34] MAN: Ours offers more, Ms. Nash. For Greek island holidays, the limit is ten thousand pounds.
[05:43] WOMAN: That's generous, although the whole holiday will cost us less than one thousand pounds.
[05:49] MAN: It is still wise to have adequate cover. If you need hospital treatment, the allowance is six hundred pounds.
[05:57] WOMAN: Mine is about the same.
[05:59] MAN: We also pay for a relative to travel to the resort if necessary.
[06:03] WOMAN: My policy only says that a company representative will assist.
[06:09] MAN: So that is another difference. Does it cover you if you fail to catch the plane?
[06:14] WOMAN: I can't find anything about that on the form.
[06:18] MAN: There is no missed departure cover?
[06:21] WOMAN: No. I'll make a note of yours.

[06:23] MAN: We pay up to one thousand pounds depending on why the flight was missed. Cover for personal belongings is especially good. Up to three thousand pounds overall, with a maximum of five hundred pounds for any single item.
[06:39] WOMAN: In that case, perhaps I shouldn't take my laptop.
[06:42] MAN: Not unless you arrange separate insurance for it.
[06:46] WOMAN: Thank you. You've been very helpful. If I need to call again, what is your name?
[06:51] MAN: Ben Ludlow. That's L-U-D-L-O-W. I'm the assistant manager. My direct number is 08126-0543216.
[07:04] WOMAN: I have 08126567294 written down. Isn't that your number?
[07:11] MAN: That is the main switchboard. The number I gave you comes straight to me.
[07:15] WOMAN: I see. Thank you.

content: FeatureSizeBiggest challengeTarget age groupRailway1.2 kmconstructing tunnelsGo-kart arena[ _____ ] m²removing mounds from the track[ _____ ] year-olds
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a radio presenter interviewing a founder of Windridge Forest Railway Park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 13. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 13. In the second program in our series on local businesses, we're joined by Simon Windridge, who helped establish the highly successful Windridge Forest Railway Park.
[01:04] AUDIO: Welcome, Simon. Could you begin by explaining how the park came about? Certainly. In the 1970s, my wife Liz and I bought 80 acres of land used for sheep farming.

[01:17] AUDIO: We settled there and had two children, Sarah and Duncan. It was a marvelous place for them to grow up and they were both fascinated by trains. Over time, they created a huge system of miniature railway track. I started making larger model engines, but we never considered turning the idea into a business until I visited a theme park near Birmingham.
[01:43] AUDIO: I came away convinced that we could produce something better ourselves. So that visit gave you the idea? Exactly. We developed a small park around the miniature railway.

[01:55] AUDIO: In our first year, 1984, we admitted visitors for only one month, July, which is usually our driest month. The children were worried that people would have an unpleasant day if it rained. I managed the park while Liz continued running the farm. And the venture succeeded very quickly.

[02:17] AUDIO: It did. We lengthened the railway and made its surroundings more attractive. We planted trees which brought in more wildlife and cut sections of track through the rock. How large is the operation now?

[02:33] AUDIO: We now open throughout the year and Windridge has become one of the area's leading visitor attractions. About 50,000 people come annually and since the park began, the total has reached one and a half million. Before you hear the rest of the interview, you have some time to look at questions 14 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 14 to 20.

[03:38] AUDIO: Those numbers forced us to expand and the park is now very much a family enterprise. I'm approaching retirement so these days I concentrate on the machinery and make sure the engines keep working. Liz puts all her effort into recruiting and supporting the large team of staff who keep the park operating smoothly. Your children work there too, don't they?

[04:03] AUDIO: Yes. After spending several years as a teacher, Sarah returned and now ensures that visitors have food and drinks. That keeps her extremely busy. Duncan has been a key member of the park for the past decade.

[04:20] AUDIO: He took over construction work from me which I'll return to shortly. His new wife Judith has also joined us and is responsible for the shop. Retail is growing rapidly because so many visitors want souvenirs. Have you stopped developing the site for the time being?

[04:39] AUDIO: Not at all. We're always considering new ways to give visitors more to do. The railway is still the heart of the park and we have laid 1.2 kilometers of track so far, but we want to extend it. The local geology makes tunnel construction our greatest challenge, although we are gradually dealing with it.

[05:04] AUDIO: We're also delighted with the new go-kart arena which covers 120 square meters. Geology caused difficulties there as well because several mounds had to be removed from the track for safety. We designed the arena for children aged 5 to 12. The most popular vehicle is the Formula One cart and children have even argued over whose turn it is.
[05:31] AUDIO: And then finally to our most recent development which is the landscape. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a university tutor discussing dissertation planning and study skills with a student called Caroline. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 23. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 23.
[00:56] TUTOR: Caroline, come in and take a seat.
[00:58] CAROLINE: Thank you.
[00:59] TUTOR: How are your dissertation plans progressing?
[01:01] CAROLINE: To be honest, Dr. Schulman, I'm still struggling to settle on a title.
[01:07] TUTOR: That's quite normal at this point. One purpose of these tutorials is to help you make that decision.
[01:14] CAROLINE: Right.
[01:15] TUTOR: Let's note down a few things that may guide you. You have already selected a broad subject area, haven't you?
[01:22] CAROLINE: Yes, I want to focus on the fishing industry.
[01:25] TUTOR: I remember that was one of the fields you were considering. Which parts of the course do you feel most confident about?
[01:33] CAROLINE: I'm doing well in statistics, and I find it interesting rather than tedious.
[01:39] TUTOR: Good. Anything else?
[01:42] CAROLINE: Computer modeling really appeals to me. I can follow the material without difficulty, although several people in my class find it hard.
[01:51] TUTOR: Those sound like useful elements to include in the dissertation. Could you bring them into your research?
[01:59] CAROLINE: I'd like to, but I can't yet see how to combine them. I also feel that I don't know enough background material.
[02:07] TUTOR: I understand. How effective are your notes?
[02:11] CAROLINE: Note-taking is one of my weakest skills. My teachers used to point that out as well.
[02:16] TUTOR: Then you should deal with those weaknesses before moving much further.
[02:21] CAROLINE: What would you recommend? Before you hear the rest of the tutorial, you have some time to look at questions 24 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 24 to 30.
[03:12] TUTOR: I can talk you through several possible approaches, and you can decide which ones might suit you.
[03:18] CAROLINE: That would be helpful.
[03:20] TUTOR: Some students organize discussions with their peers. Each week, one member researches a separate topic and explains it to the rest of the group.
[03:31] CAROLINE: I see.
[03:33] TUTOR: Presenting material to other people can do a great deal to increase your confidence.
[03:38] CAROLINE: That makes sense.
[03:39] TUTOR: The disadvantage is that members of a group often exchange the same ideas, and those ideas then appear repeatedly in everyone's dissertation.
[03:51] CAROLINE: Yes, that could be a problem.
[03:53] TUTOR: Another option is a service called Student Support. It provides a structured program lasting several weeks to improve academic skills.
[04:04] CAROLINE: That sounds useful.
[04:05] TUTOR: It is, but only a limited number of places are available. Even so, it is worth investigating.
[04:13] CAROLINE: Definitely. I know my study methods need attention.
[04:18] TUTOR: You could also consult some of the books on study skills.
[04:22] CAROLINE: All right.
[04:23] TUTOR: They can be valuable for reference, but their advice is sometimes too general.
[04:29] CAROLINE: Yes, I've noticed that myself.
[04:32] TUTOR: Apart from those options, I strongly recommend a few simple techniques, such as keeping a card index.
[04:40] CAROLINE: I've never tried that.

[04:42] TUTOR: It is straightforward but effective, because it forces you to record each point in a small space. I also tell students not to put their notes away and forget them. Read every set of notes three times. That helps the information stay in your memory.
[04:59] CAROLINE: I can see the benefit, although it would require discipline.
[05:04] TUTOR: If you develop strong study habits now, they will remain useful throughout your life.
[05:10] CAROLINE: I agree. My difficulty is making myself follow a routine. I find it helpful to discuss things with someone.
[05:19] TUTOR: We'll continue these tutorials, of course. Let's arrange the next one now. I'm available at almost any time in the week, beginning January 22nd.
[05:30] CAROLINE: Could we meet on the 24th? I'm free that afternoon.
[05:35] TUTOR: I'm afraid I already have an appointment then. How about the day after?
[05:40] CAROLINE: Thursday the 25th? I could come in the morning.
[05:44] TUTOR: Good. Let's make it the 25th.
[05:47] CAROLINE: Excellent. Thank you.
[05:52] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: The Underground House
content: 📌 THE UNDERGROUND HOUSE
Design
Built within the earth on two floorsThe south-facing side was made from two layers of [ _____ ]Photovoltaic tiles were attached to the wallFoam was added for better [ _____ ]
Special features

Many internal mirrors and [ _____ ] increase the available lightThe house may eventually generate more [ _____ ] than it usesRecycled wood was used for the [ _____ ]Domestic [ _____ ] is treated organically
Environmental issues
Using a large amount of [ _____ ] during construction harmed the environmentThe house will repay its “environmental debt” within [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer describing the design and environmental impact of an underground house. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Good morning.

[00:54] AUDIO: In recent lectures we have examined the historical development of house construction. Today I'm going to turn to modern experimental housing, beginning with a home built almost entirely beneath the ground. An interesting aspect of the project is the involvement of its owners. Both had professional careers, although neither was an architect, and they wanted to take an active role, so they managed the project themselves.

[01:24] AUDIO: Their main objective was to build a home with the smallest possible environmental impact. They also wanted a quiet place to live. Both had grown up in the countryside and did not enjoy urban life. Their first task was to find a suitable location.

[01:46] AUDIO: They eventually bought an abandoned stone quarry in an attractive area. The land was comparatively inexpensive and reusing it appealed to them. At that point the quarry was an unattractive mark on the landscape and no longer served any productive purpose. After consulting several architects and considering a range of plans, the owners selected an underground design.

[02:16] AUDIO: The house was constructed within the earth on two levels. Its northern, eastern, and western sides were buried, while only the sloping side facing south remained open to daylight. This exposed side consists of two layers of extremely strong glass. Photovoltaic tiles were fixed along the upper and lower parts of the sloping wall.

[02:42] AUDIO: These tiles collect energy from sunlight. The walls were also surrounded by foam to improve the building's insulation. For us, the most significant aspect of the project is the collection of features that make the house energy efficient. Daylight enters through the glass wall and numerous mirrors and windows inside distribute it throughout the rooms.

[03:11] AUDIO: In this way, the available natural light is used as fully as possible. The exterior tiles also transform solar energy into electricity for the house. In future, the system may generate more electricity than the occupants require, allowing them to sell the excess to the national grid. Recycled materials were used whenever possible.

[03:37] AUDIO: The floors, for instance, were made from reclaimed wood. The owners also bought no new furniture and continued using what they already possessed. Another important feature is the method used to deal with domestic waste. The waste is processed organically.

[03:57] AUDIO: It is purified as it passes through reed beds planted in the garden for this purpose. As a result, the household avoids polluting the ground or relying on harmful chemicals. We should acknowledge that constructing the house initially damaged the environment. The principal reason was the enormous quantity of concrete required.

[04:22] AUDIO: Manufacturing concrete releases substantial amounts of carbon dioxide, and the building process produced a total of seventy tons of it. That figure is alarming. However, calculations show that the original environmental debt will be repaid in only fifteen years. After that, the underground house will have no continuing environmental cost because, unlike a conventional home, it operates in a completely sustainable manner.
[04:57] AUDIO: So, eco-housing of this kind is likely to become much more... That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man asking for information about local health centers. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:50] WOMAN: How can I help you?
[00:52] MAN: My wife, our children, and I have just moved into the area and I'd like to find a health center where we can all register with the doctor.
[01:00] WOMAN: Certainly. At the Harvey Clinic, there's Dr. Green. We normally recommend her for babies because she works particularly well with them and runs a specialist clinic.
[01:11] MAN: My youngest is already five, so that probably wouldn't be useful for us.
[01:17] WOMAN: I see.
[01:18] MAN: Is there another center I could consider?
[01:21] WOMAN: The next one on my list is the Eshcol Health Practice.
[01:26] MAN: Could you spell Eshcol?
[01:27] WOMAN: E-S-H-C-O-L. Dr. Fuller is accepting new patients there. The practice opened only a year ago, so all the equipment and facilities are very modern.
[01:43] MAN: That sounds promising.

[01:44] WOMAN: It's especially convenient for people who are occupied during the day because evening appointments are available. However, the practice doesn't open on Saturdays. The final option is the health center in Shore Lane. You could register with Dr. Gormley.
[02:03] WOMAN: G-O-R-M-L-E-Y. He has only recently joined, but the center itself has an excellent reputation.
[02:13] MAN: I think I know Shore Lane. That would probably suit us best. Are all its services provided free?

[02:21] WOMAN: Doctors sometimes charge small fees for particular services. Let me check the information for Shore Lane. Vaccinations required for travel abroad are free. Treatment for sports injuries has to be paid for, and so does nutritional therapy.

[02:38] WOMAN: Some centers include alternative treatments such as homeopathy among their paid services. Shore Lane hopes to introduce something similar. Perhaps starting with acupuncture. The center also gives free health checks for people who need to show a new employer that they are fit and have no serious previous injuries.
[03:01] WOMAN: Insurance medical examinations, however, usually involve a charge.
[03:06] MAN: Alright, thank you.
[03:11] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
[03:56] WOMAN: You may also like to know that the center is testing a program of talks for patients. I have the schedule here and several of the sessions look worthwhile.
[04:06] MAN: What subjects do they cover?

[04:09] WOMAN: The first talk is about stopping smoking. It's next week on February 25th at 7 in the evening in room 4. The description says it will emphasize the health advantages, particularly for anyone with asthma or heart problems.
[04:26] MAN: That sounds useful.
[04:28] WOMAN: There is also a session for families with children on healthy eating. It will be held on March 1st at 5 o'clock.
[04:36] MAN: Is that taking place at the health center?
[04:39] WOMAN: No, it's at the primary school in Shore Lane. They may be expecting parents whose children attend the school. Although the notice says everyone is welcome.
[04:50] MAN: I might attend if I'm free.

[04:53] WOMAN: Another talk explains how to prevent injuries while exercising. It's on March 9th in the late afternoon at 4.30 and it will be in room 6. The session is suitable for all ages. The final talk is called Stress Management, which is...
[05:14] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Water Heater
content:
Best place to park in town: beside the station
Telephone number for pizza takeaway: [ _____ ]
Railway museum closed on: [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a woman telephoning the owner of a holiday flat for help with its heating system. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 13. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 13. Hello?

[00:53] AUDIO: Hi, Laura Caraton speaking. We've just reached the holiday flat but I can't make the heating or hot water work. That's simple to sort out, so don't worry. The water heater is in the upstairs cupboard.

[01:06] AUDIO: At the lower left of the unit, you'll see three main controls. The round control on the far left is the most important because it's the main on and off switch for both the heating and the hot water. Check that it's set to on. It has probably been turned off accidentally.

[01:26] AUDIO: The middle control is slightly larger and operates the radiators. If the flat feels cold and you want them on, turn that control up to its highest setting. The control on the right normally stays at about four, which should make the tap water hot enough. Beneath those controls in the center, there's a small circular plastic button.

[01:51] AUDIO: Occasionally, the heater cuts out when there isn't enough water in the pipes. If that happens, press this reset button for about five seconds and the unit should start again. Under the third control, there's also a small square warning indicator. It flashes whenever the heater needs to be reset.
[02:12] AUDIO: It sounds rather complicated. I'm sure it will be fine. More detailed instructions should be attached to the side of the heater. Phone me again if it still won't work.

[02:24] AUDIO: All right. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 14 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 14 to 20. Before you go, there are a few things we haven't been able to locate, including spare pillows and washing powder.
[03:23] AUDIO: Are they supplied? Yes. The extra pillows should be in the large white cupboard upstairs, just to the left of the bathroom door. There are normally four or five on the top shelf.

[03:36] AUDIO: The washing powder is probably near the back door. There is a shelf above the sink there, and I'm certain you'll find a large blue box on it. Use about half a cup for each load. That reminds me, the spare key for the back door hangs on a hook on the wall beside the living room window.

[03:56] AUDIO: Please return it after use. The previous visitors lost it in the garden. You may also need replacement light bulbs. They're in a large cardboard box containing various useful items on top of the washing machine.
[04:12] AUDIO: There's one more thing I forgot to tell you earlier. Yes. I left a local map to help you find your way around. It covers the whole district.

[04:22] AUDIO: You'll find it in the top drawer of the chest beneath the television in your bedroom, together with a file of local information. Thank you. Do you have any suggestions for visiting the town? You'll need to drive because it's too far to walk from the flat.

[04:40] AUDIO: Unfortunately, every car park now charges. I prefer the one beside the station. The town center is only a five-minute walk from there, and that's where the best restaurants are. If you'd rather order food, the Italian takeaway makes excellent pasta and pizza.
[04:57] AUDIO: Its number is 732281. The Chinese restaurant is also good. Its number is 766119. Both places deliver to the flat.

[05:12] AUDIO: You should also visit the railway museum. The exhibition isn't large, but it's very good. Sundays are extremely busy, so a quieter day later in the week is better. Don't go on Thursday, though.
[05:27] AUDIO: It's market day. Parking is impossible, and Thursday is the only day when the museum is closed. Is there anything else? Not at the moment.
[05:38] AUDIO: Thanks very much. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Kira - The Exchange Student
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Kira - The Exchange Student"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear Paul interviewing Kira about her experience as an overseas university student. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:53] PAUL: Hello, Kira. How are you?
[00:56] KIRA: I'm well. Thanks, Paul. And you?
[00:59] PAUL: Very well. It's good to see you again. Has it been a full year since you took our course?
[01:07] KIRA: Yes, it has. It's nice to return for a visit.
[01:11] PAUL: Which course did you enroll on?
[01:14] KIRA: I actually entered the third year of pharmacy straight away. The university gave me credit for two years, although going directly into the final stage probably made things harder.
[01:27] PAUL: Receiving those credits was fortunate, though. Was that the reason you selected pharmacy?
[01:34] KIRA: Yes. I had already completed a pharmacy course in my own country, so I expected a familiar subject to be easier.

[01:43] PAUL: I didn't know you had joined the third year. I assumed you began in year one. That explains why it was such a challenge. What was one major difference between studying here and studying at home?

[01:59] KIRA: Writing assignments was very difficult because that part of the system was unfamiliar to me. The biggest issue was that lecturers expected critical analysis. I felt awful at first. I wondered how I could possibly judge another researcher's work when that person might have spent five years on it.

[02:21] KIRA: Many international students probably faced the same difficulty. It became more manageable with time. People often assume the problem will be reading or writing quickly enough, but the real requirement is to change the way you think about academic work.
[02:37] PAUL: What about the subject matter in the lectures? Could you understand it?
[02:44] KIRA: Yes. The material closely resembled what I had studied before, so following the lectures wasn't a major problem.
[02:53] PAUL: Were the lecturers similar to those in your country?

[02:57] KIRA: Not really. The lecturers here are much easier to approach. After a lecture, you can ask about anything you failed to understand, or arrange an appointment to discuss any part of the course.
[03:12] PAUL: Perhaps they seem different because you're more mature now than you were during your earlier studies, when you may have been less confident.

[03:22] KIRA: I don't think that explains it. Most students here contact their lecturers. In my faculty, students regularly book appointments, usually because something on the course worries them, but sometimes because a topic interests them greatly, and they may want to specialise in it. Lecturers have to reserve certain periods each week for student meetings.
[03:48] PAUL: That's encouraging.
[03:53] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the interview, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[04:38] PAUL: What was your timetable like? Was the year very demanding?

[04:44] KIRA: Extremely demanding. We were expected to work hard. In addition to lectures, we had practical classes in many subjects, and we completed those sessions in small groups. Every week, I also spent four hours working in a community pharmacy.

[05:03] KIRA: I enjoyed that because I was constantly meeting new people. During the second semester, we needed experience in hospital dispensaries, so we worked in one of the large hospitals every second day. We still had to complete all our assignments, which took me a long time. And between the first and second semesters, we worked full-time in a hospital for two weeks.
[05:29] PAUL: That certainly sounds like an exhausting year. Are you glad you completed it? Do you feel you achieved something?
[05:38] KIRA: Yes. Above all, I feel much more confident now.
[05:43] PAUL: What advice would you offer students arriving from other countries?

[05:48] KIRA: They need a very strong command of English. It would help if they spent longer improving it before entering university. If you can't understand what people are saying and have no time to translate, you can get into serious difficulty.
[06:04] PAUL: Is there anything else?
[06:05] KIRA: As I mentioned earlier, my greatest problem was not being familiar with the education system here.
[06:13] PAUL: It sounds as though the year tested you in many ways. Congratulations, Kira.
[06:20] KIRA: Thank you, Paul.
[06:24] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a student presenting a research project on wildlife in urban gardens. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Good morning.

[00:53] AUDIO: Today I'm going to report the findings from our second year project on wildlife living in gardens across the city. I'll begin with the background to the project, describe our research methods, and then outline some of our preliminary results. To start with, why did we select this subject? There are four students in our group.

[01:17] AUDIO: While we were discussing possible topics, two members said they had noticed still more sparrow hawks. One of Britain's most fascinating birds of prey, appearing in their own city center gardens. They wondered why these birds had begun arriving in such large numbers. That led all of us to become interested in the broader question of why wild creatures choose urban gardens as habitats.

[01:46] AUDIO: Why have gardens become increasingly attractive to wildlife while the countryside itself appears less suitable? Our first step was to calculate how much urban land consists of private gardens. We initially estimated about one-fifth. We then checked large-scale land use maps held by the town survey office, which confirmed a precise figure of 24 percent.

[02:17] AUDIO: Informal conversations with friends and neighbors suggested that many householders had interesting wildlife observations to share. We therefore surveyed garden owners in several districts of the city. Slightly more than 100 participants completed a survey every two weeks for an entire year. They marked the species they had observed on a prepared list and added the names of any less common animals.

[02:47] AUDIO: At the same time, our group carried out observations in selected gardens across the city. We deliberately used smaller gardens because these were much more representative of the typical garden here. The aim was to investigate ordinary conditions rather than unusual examples. Alongside this fieldwork, we read extensively about the decline of wildlife in rural areas and considered the possible causes.

[03:19] AUDIO: Our findings were far too extensive to cover completely today. Anyone who wants more detail can view the graphs on the college website, and members of the group are also happy to discuss the research by e-mail. For this presentation, we selected three species because they provide the clearest indication of the general processes operating in both rural and urban environments. The first species that produced particularly interesting evidence was the frog.

[03:56] AUDIO: The pattern was unmistakable. Frogs multiply wherever appropriate stretches of water are available. Garden ponds are becoming more common while rural ponds are disappearing, causing a substantial movement of frogs into towns. Hedgehogs also survive more successfully in cities.

[04:19] AUDIO: Their predators are less willing to leave rural habitats, so urban hedgehogs face less danger and have a higher survival rate. We received a great many sightings, which made it easy to count their numbers accurately. The final species is one of the finest singing birds, the song Thrush. Its rural population is falling, but it is recovering in city gardens.

[04:48] AUDIO: Modern gardeners grow many different plants, producing a wide variety of seeds for the birds to eat. Gardens also provide more nesting locations than the countryside. That may sound surprising, but the evidence supports it. We also discovered that a major new survey of song thrushes is about to begin, so watch for further information.
[05:15] AUDIO: I'd now be pleased to answer any questions. That is the end of part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
